subject: ELA
overview: English 11 moves chronologically through American literature, pairing each period's fiction and poetry with the speeches and essays that shaped it. A typical 60-minute day is 25–30 minutes of reading (often aloud together), 15–20 minutes of annotation or discussion, and 10–15 minutes of writing. Push every claim back to the text ('Show me the line'), keep the reading journal going all year, and treat each essay as a draft-feedback-revise cycle. Many texts are free on Project Gutenberg, CommonLit, and Poetry Foundation; preview the flagged mature content.

weeks.prep: Get a composition notebook for the reading journal. Find 'The World on the Turtle's Back' (Iroquois creation story, widely anthologized) and William Bradford's Of Plymouth Plantation, Book I ch. 9–10 and Book II's first-winter section (Gutenberg). Preview both.
misconceptions: Treating a creation story as 'just a myth' with no argument. Show that it teaches values (balance of good and evil, cooperation of animals, respect for earth) just as Bradford's history does.
Writing an 'objective summary' that includes opinions ('this beautiful story'). An objective summary states who/what/what happened and the central idea, with no judgments.

days.guide: Explain the reading journal: date, title, a quotation, and a response each day. Then set a 20-minute timer for the diagnostic on 'What makes someone an American?' without help. Read it afterward only to note strengths and one goal; do not grade it.

questions.q: What two things should every journal entry include?
questions.a: A quotation (with page or paragraph) and the student's own response or question about it.

days.guide: Read the story aloud together. Have the student annotate values in the margin (e.g., the animals working together, the twins representing good and evil), then write a 150-word summary with no opinions. Check: could someone who never read it understand the plot from the summary?

questions.q: How is the earth created in 'The World on the Turtle's Back'?
questions.a: The sky woman falls from the sky world through a hole by an uprooted tree; water animals dive for earth, and the mud one brings up is spread on the turtle's back, which grows into the land.

questions.q: What do the twins represent?
questions.a: Opposing forces in the world: the good-minded twin creates useful and beautiful things, and the evil-minded twin creates harmful things, so the world holds a balance of both.

days.guide: Read Bradford's account of the voyage and first winter aloud. Have the student make a chart: event | how Bradford explains it. Point out that he credits God's 'providence' for both the deaths of enemies and the survival of the Pilgrims.

questions.q: How does Bradford explain the death of the 'proud and very profane' young sailor who cursed the sick passengers?
questions.a: As God's judgment: it 'pleased God' to strike him with a grievous disease so he was the first to die, which Bradford calls 'the just hand of God upon him.'

questions.q: What did the Pilgrims do when they first reached land, and what does it show?
questions.a: They 'fell upon their knees and blessed the God of heaven' who had brought them safely; it shows their belief that God directed every event (providence).

days.guide: Model one row of the two-column chart (nature: in the creation story the earth is a living gift built by animal cooperation; for Bradford the land is a 'hideous and desolate wilderness'). The student completes the chart, then makes 10 vocabulary cards using roots (provid- 'foresee', -cracy, etc.).

questions.q: Contrast how the two texts view nature.
questions.a: The Iroquois story presents nature as sacred and cooperative, with animals as helpers; Bradford sees the New England wilderness as hostile and desolate, something to endure and tame with God's help.

days.guide: Timed paragraph (25 min): how does each text explain hardship? Require two quotations from each. Then give a 10-term quiz (Puritan, providence, plain style, covenant, predestination, worldview, etc.).

questions.q: Define 'plain style.'
questions.a: The Puritan writing style that uses simple, direct language and avoids ornament, because the goal was clarity and truth for God's glory, not display.

weeks.assessment_key: Paragraph rubric (4-point): 4 = clear comparative topic sentence; two accurate quotations from each text; explains that Bradford attributes hardship to God's providence/testing while the creation story frames struggle as part of the balance between creative and destructive forces; objective summary is accurate. 3 = all parts present, analysis thinner. 2 = quotations but little comparison. 1 = summary only. Vocabulary quiz key: Puritan = English Protestants seeking to 'purify' the Church; providence = God's guidance of all events; plain style = simple, direct writing; worldview = a set of beliefs used to interpret the world; predestination = belief that God has already chosen who is saved; covenant = a binding agreement (with God or among people, e.g., the Mayflower Compact).

weeks.prep: Print Bradstreet's 'To My Dear and Loving Husband' and 'Upon the Burning of Our House' and Edwards' 'Sinners in the Hands of an Angry God' (CommonLit/Gutenberg). Make a SOAPSTone chart (Speaker, Occasion, Audience, Purpose, Subject, Tone). Have a phone ready to record Day 5.
misconceptions: Reading Edwards as a hateful man rather than analyzing his purpose. Ask: what did he want listeners to DO? (Seek salvation now.) Analysis means explaining choices, not just reacting.
Labeling every vivid image 'pathos' without explaining the emotion. Have the student name the specific emotion (terror, urgency) and why it moves this audience.

days.guide: Read both poems aloud twice. Model annotating the metaphor of love as wealth ('more than whole mines of gold'), then have the student find the conflict in the house poem: grief for lost belongings versus the lesson that true treasure is in heaven.

questions.q: In 'Upon the Burning of Our House,' how does Bradstreet resolve her grief?
questions.a: She reminds herself that earthly goods are 'mould'ring dust' and that she has a better house in heaven: 'My hope and treasure lies above.'

questions.q: What metaphor dominates 'To My Dear and Loving Husband'?
questions.a: Love as riches/debt: she prizes his love 'more than whole mines of gold' and says she can never repay it, so she prays the heavens will reward him.

days.guide: Read the first half aloud with emphasis. The student highlights images (spider, fire, flood/dammed waters, bent bow) and labels each with the appeal and emotion.

questions.q: What is the effect of the spider image?
questions.a: God holds the sinner 'much as one holds a spider, or some loathsome insect, over the fire'; it makes listeners feel small, helpless, and in immediate danger, which creates terror (pathos).

days.guide: Finish the sermon. Fill SOAPSTone together for Speaker and Occasion (Edwards, Enfield, Connecticut, 1741, during the Great Awakening), then let the student finish and explain why fear worked.

questions.q: Why was fear effective for Edwards' 1741 audience?
questions.a: They already believed in hell and God's judgment; Edwards made that belief feel immediate and personal, so terror pushed them to seek conversion right away, during the revival of the Great Awakening.

questions.q: What hope does Edwards offer at the end?
questions.a: That Christ 'has thrown the door of mercy wide open' now; listeners can still be saved if they turn to God immediately.

days.guide: Explain periodic sentences (main point delayed to the end) and cumulative sentences (main clause first, details added). Find one long Edwards sentence and mark where the main clause lands; the student rewrites three of their own sentences both ways.

questions.q: Turn this into a periodic sentence: 'I finished the race even though I was exhausted and my shoe was untied.'
questions.a: Example: 'Exhausted, shoe untied, gasping for every breath, I finished the race.' (The main clause comes last.)

days.guide: Record a 15-minute discussion on 'Is fear a legitimate persuasive tool?' The parent should push back once; the student must cite Edwards at least twice. Collect the SOAPSTone chart.

questions.q: Give one argument that fear can be legitimate persuasion.
questions.a: When the danger is real (e.g., public-health warnings), fear can motivate protective action; it becomes manipulation when it exaggerates or replaces reasons.

weeks.assessment_key: SOAPSTone key: Speaker = Jonathan Edwards, Puritan minister; Occasion = sermon at Enfield, CT, 1741, Great Awakening revival; Audience = a congregation he believed complacent about salvation; Purpose = to frighten them into seeking conversion now; Subject = sinners' precarious position before an angry God; Tone = urgent, threatening, then pleading. Discussion rubric (4-point): 4 = cites the text accurately at least twice, responds directly to the other speaker's points, extends or challenges ideas with reasons; 3 = cites once or twice and responds; 2 = opinions with little evidence; 1 = minimal participation.

weeks.prep: Arthur Miller's The Crucible (library). Short readings: an encyclopedia article on the 1692 Salem witch trials and one on HUAC/McCarthyism. Parent note: the play involves an adulterous affair (discussed, not shown).
misconceptions: Treating the play as an accurate history of Salem. Miller changed facts (e.g., Abigail was about 11 in reality, he made her 17 and invented the affair) to explore 1950s fears; check his note 'A Note on the Historical Accuracy of This Play.'
Missing that characters act from motives beyond fear of witches. Have the student track land, reputation, and revenge (Putnam wants land; Parris fears for his position; Abigail wants Elizabeth gone).

days.guide: Read both short articles. The student lists parallels in a T-chart: accusations without evidence, pressure to name others, confession rewarded, reputations ruined.

questions.q: Name two parallels Miller saw between Salem and the 1950s HUAC hearings.
questions.a: In both, people were pressured to confess and name others to save themselves, and accusations were treated as proof (guilt by association), destroying reputations.

days.guide: Read Act I aloud, each of you taking several roles. The student fills a motive chart for Abigail, Parris, Putnam, and Proctor. Today's task from the plan: Read Act I aloud, taking several roles; track each character's motives (Abigail, Parris, Putnam, Proctor) in a chart. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: What does Abigail want in Act I?
questions.a: To avoid punishment for the forest dancing and to get John Proctor back; she resents Elizabeth Proctor, who dismissed her.

questions.q: Why is Parris so worried about the rumors?
questions.a: He fears that witchcraft in his own house will cost him his reputation and his position as minister.

days.guide: Reread Miller's stage-direction introduction of John Proctor. Model one sentence of analysis, then the student writes a paragraph on how the description (powerful, even-tempered, a sinner against his own sense of decency) prepares us for his conflict.

questions.q: What key trait does Miller give Proctor in the stage directions?
questions.a: He is respected and strong but sees himself as a sinner (a 'fraud') because of his affair, so he carries private guilt.

days.guide: Read Act II. Define dramatic irony (the audience knows something a character does not). The student finds three moments and explains the poppet. Today's task from the plan: Read Act II; identify three moments of dramatic irony and explain the poppet's role in the plot. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: What role does the poppet play in the plot?
questions.a: Mary Warren made it in court and gave it to Elizabeth; Abigail stabs herself with a needle and claims Elizabeth's spirit did it, so the needle in the poppet becomes 'evidence' to arrest Elizabeth.

questions.q: Give one example of dramatic irony in Act II.
questions.a: Cheever and Herrick treat the needle as proof of witchcraft, but the audience knows Mary Warren put it there and Abigail is faking.

days.guide: Give a 10-question reading quiz, then the student writes a prediction paragraph for Act III supported by two quotations. Today's task from the plan: Reading quiz on Acts I–II and a one-paragraph prediction defended with evidence. Grade it the same day with the key below and have the student correct every missed item with a one-line note on what went wrong.

questions.q: At the end of Act II, what does Proctor insist Mary Warren must do?
questions.a: Testify in court that the poppet was hers and that Abigail's accusations are false.

weeks.assessment_key: Reading quiz key (10 items): 1) Salem, Massachusetts, 1692. 2) Betty Parris is the girl who won't wake. 3) The girls were dancing in the forest with Tituba. 4) Abigail had an affair with John Proctor. 5) Elizabeth fired Abigail. 6) Thomas Putnam is motivated by land and grudges. 7) Reverend Hale is the 'expert' on witchcraft. 8) When Hale tests Proctor, he can't recall the commandment against adultery (Elizabeth supplies it). 9) Mary Warren gives Elizabeth the poppet. 10) Elizabeth is arrested. Characterization paragraph rubric (4-point): topic sentence about Proctor's trait; two stage-direction or dialogue quotations; explanation of how the description creates his conflict; conventions.

weeks.prep: Finish The Crucible. Find the courtroom scene of the 1996 film (Daniel Day-Lewis, Winona Ryder). Print a literary argument rubric and a counterclaim template.
misconceptions: Calling Proctor a tragic hero without defining the term. Use Aristotle's features: a person of stature, a tragic flaw, a reversal and recognition, and a downfall that brings insight.
Ignoring the counterclaim or 'straw-manning' it. A strong counterclaim is a real objection (e.g., Proctor's lust and delay helped cause the tragedy) answered with evidence.

days.guide: Read Act III. The student tracks how logic breaks down (Danforth: a witness is either for the court or against it) and finds where Hale turns. Today's task from the plan: Read the courtroom act; trace how logic breaks down and cite the line where Hale turns. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: Where does Hale turn against the court?
questions.a: After Elizabeth denies the affair and Mary Warren accuses Proctor, Hale cries, 'I denounce these proceedings, I quit this court!'

questions.q: Why does Elizabeth's lie in Act III backfire?
questions.a: Proctor had confessed the affair to discredit Abigail; Elizabeth, never known to lie, denies it to protect his name, which makes Proctor look like a liar.

days.guide: Read Act IV. Discuss why Proctor tears up his confession. The student drafts a one-sentence thesis on integrity. Today's task from the plan: Read Act IV; discuss why Proctor refuses to sign and what 'my name' means; draft a thesis on integrity. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: Why does Proctor refuse to let his signed confession be posted?
questions.a: 'Because it is my name! Because I cannot have another in my life!' A public lie would destroy his integrity and betray those who died honestly.

questions.q: What does Elizabeth mean by 'He have his goodness now'?
questions.a: By choosing death over a lie, Proctor has finally regained his self-respect and goodness, which she will not take from him.

days.guide: Watch the film's courtroom scene with the script open. The student notes two staging choices about Abigail's power (camera, the girls' mimicry, her stare) and whether they match Miller's directions.

questions.q: How does the 'yellow bird' scene show Abigail's power?
questions.a: Abigail claims to see Mary Warren's spirit as a bird; the other girls copy everything Mary says, so the court sees 'proof' and Mary breaks, showing Abigail controls the room.

days.guide: Review the rubric and a model counterclaim paragraph. The student writes the 700-word essay, then edits for subject-verb agreement (e.g., 'The girls, led by Abigail, are...').

questions.q: Correct: 'Each of the accused girls were afraid.'
questions.a: 'Each of the accused girls was afraid.' (The subject 'each' is singular.)

days.guide: The student revises with the checklist (thesis, counterclaim, citations), then takes the Unit 1 test. Today's task from the plan: Revise essay with a checklist and take the Unit 1 test (passages from Edwards and Miller). Grade it the same day with the key below and have the student correct every missed item with a one-line note on what went wrong.

questions.q: What is a tragic hero?
questions.a: A person of stature with a tragic flaw whose choices lead to downfall, often with recognition (insight) before the end.

weeks.assessment_key: Literary argument rubric (4 = exceeds, 3 = proficient, 2 = developing, 1 = beginning) on four rows: Claim/Thesis (arguable, specific, answers the prompt); Evidence (well-chosen quotations, introduced and cited); Analysis/Reasoning (explains HOW evidence supports the claim, not just what it says); Conventions & organization (logical paragraphs, transitions, few errors). A proficient (3) paper has a clear yes/no thesis about Proctor as tragic hero, uses at least three quotations (e.g., his confession in Act III, 'Because it is my name!' in Act IV), explains his flaw (pride/lust and his delay) and recognition, and answers a genuine counterclaim. Unit 1 test key: Edwards' purpose = frighten listeners into conversion; spider image = pathos/helplessness; providence = God's guidance; Miller's allegory = McCarthyism; dramatic irony = audience knows Abigail is lying; Hale's change = from confident expert to opponent of the court.

weeks.prep: Franklin's Autobiography, Part II ('arriving at moral perfection') and Poor Richard's Almanack sayings (Gutenberg); 'Remarks Concerning the Savages of North America' (Gutenberg/CommonLit).
misconceptions: Thinking Franklin's tone toward himself is entirely serious. Point out his self-deprecating humor, e.g., he admits he gained more of the 'appearance' of humility than the reality.
Confusing verbal irony with sarcasm or coincidence. Verbal irony is saying the opposite of what one means; in 'Remarks' the 'Savages' are shown to be more civil than the English.

days.guide: Read the moral-perfection section. The student lists the 13 virtues and marks two places where Franklin laughs at himself. Today's task from the plan: Read Franklin's 'project of arriving at moral perfection'; list his 13 virtues and mark his tone toward himself. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: List Franklin's 13 virtues.
questions.a: Temperance, Silence, Order, Resolution, Frugality, Industry, Sincerity, Justice, Moderation, Cleanliness, Tranquility, Chastity, Humility.

questions.q: Why did Franklin add Humility?
questions.a: A Quaker friend told him he was considered proud; he says he had little success with the reality of humility but a good deal with its appearance.

days.guide: Read 20 aphorisms. Model one ('Early to bed and early to rise, makes a man healthy, wealthy, and wise' assumes discipline produces success). The student rewrites five.

questions.q: What assumption lies behind 'God helps them that help themselves'?
questions.a: That success comes from personal effort and that individuals are responsible for improving their own lives, an Enlightenment and self-made-man value.

days.guide: Read 'Remarks.' Model the first line's irony, then the student finds two more examples and names the target (English/colonial arrogance). Today's task from the plan: Read 'Remarks Concerning the Savages of North America'; identify verbal irony and its target. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: What is ironic about the opening 'Savages we call them, because their manners differ from ours'?
questions.a: Franklin shows the label is based only on difference, not merit; he then presents Native customs as more polite and reasonable than colonial ones, so the 'civilized' are the real target.

questions.q: How do the Native leaders respond to the offer to educate their young men at the college?
questions.a: They politely decline, saying their youths who were educated came back useless as hunters or warriors, and offer instead to educate a dozen Virginians' sons and 'make men of them.'

days.guide: The student tracks one virtue for three days in a Franklin-style chart, then drafts a 400-word reflective explanation (what they tried, results, what it shows about self-improvement).

questions.q: What should the reflection explain beyond 'I did it'?
questions.a: What specific behavior was tracked, the results (data from the chart), what was difficult, and what the experiment suggests about Franklin's method.

days.guide: Give a short-answer quiz on Enlightenment ideas (reason, progress, self-improvement, deism) and irony. Collect the reflection. Grade it the same day with the key below and have the student correct every missed item with a one-line note on what went wrong.

questions.q: Name two Enlightenment values Franklin's writing shows.
questions.a: Faith in reason/rational method (his chart system) and belief in self-improvement and progress through human effort.

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz key: 1) Enlightenment = 18th-century movement valuing reason, science, and progress. 2) Franklin's virtue chart = a rational, systematic method for moral improvement. 3) Aphorism = short, memorable statement of a general truth. 4) Verbal irony in 'Remarks' = calling Native people 'savages' while showing their superior courtesy. 5) Deism = belief in a creator who does not intervene, known through reason. Reflection rubric (4-point): specific virtue and tracking data; honest analysis of results; connection to Franklin's method; clear organization and correct conventions.

weeks.prep: Paine's Common Sense (excerpt) and The American Crisis No. 1; Patrick Henry's Speech to the Virginia Convention; the Declaration of Independence (archives.gov).
misconceptions: Thinking the Declaration's grievances are all equally strong. Have the student evaluate which are specific and verifiable and which are exaggerated or blame the King for Parliament's acts.
Missing who is excluded from 'all men are created equal.' Discuss enslaved people, women, and Native Americans (called 'merciless Indian Savages' in a grievance).

days.guide: Read the opening of The Crisis aloud. The student labels appeals and parallel structure and notes plain diction aimed at ordinary readers. Today's task from the plan: Read excerpts and label appeals and parallel structure; note how Paine addresses a mass audience. Before the student writes conclusions, check that the data table has units and repeated trials, and ask them to explain one result in their own words.

questions.q: Explain 'The summer soldier and the sunshine patriot will, in this crisis, shrink from the service of their country.'
questions.a: Paine shames those who support the cause only when it is easy; the alliteration and parallel images challenge readers to stay loyal in hard times.

days.guide: Read Henry's speech; the student delivers the final paragraph aloud. Chart rhetorical questions and allusions. Today's task from the plan: Read and deliver the final paragraph aloud; chart rhetorical questions, allusions, and their effect. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: What does 'Suffer not yourselves to be betrayed with a kiss' allude to and why?
questions.a: Judas betraying Jesus with a kiss; Henry warns that Britain's friendly gestures hide betrayal.

questions.q: What is the effect of the final rhetorical question 'Is life so dear, or peace so sweet, as to be purchased at the price of chains and slavery?'
questions.a: It forces listeners to admit that peace under tyranny is not worth it, building to 'give me liberty, or give me death!'

days.guide: Outline the Declaration as a syllogism on the board. Today's task from the plan: Outline the Declaration as a syllogism (major premise, minor premise/grievances, conclusion). Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: State the Declaration's argument as a syllogism.
questions.a: Major premise: when a government destroys people's rights, they may alter or abolish it. Minor premise: the King has repeatedly violated colonists' rights (the grievances). Conclusion: the colonies are free and independent states.

days.guide: The student picks the strongest and weakest grievance and writes a paragraph evaluating each as evidence, then a sentence on who is excluded. Today's task from the plan: Write a paragraph evaluating the strongest and weakest grievance as evidence; note who is excluded from 'all men'. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: Give one strong grievance and explain why.
questions.a: 'For imposing Taxes on us without our Consent' is specific and connects directly to the principle of consent of the governed.

days.guide: Timed 30-minute paragraph comparing how Paine and Jefferson open their texts. Today's task from the plan: Compare two openings (Paine vs. Jefferson) in a timed 30-minute rhetorical paragraph. Grade it the same day with the key below and have the student correct every missed item with a one-line note on what went wrong.

questions.q: How do the two openings differ in approach?
questions.a: Paine opens with emotional, urgent language ('These are the times that try men's souls'); Jefferson opens with calm, formal reasoning about the 'Laws of Nature' and a 'decent respect' for world opinion.

weeks.assessment_key: Timed paragraph rubric (4-point): 4 = clear claim comparing purpose and tone; quotes both openings; analyzes specific choices (Paine's emotional diction and aphorism for soldiers and common readers vs. Jefferson's formal, logical diction for a world audience); explains effect on audience. 3 = accurate comparison with less precise analysis. 2 = summary of both. 1 = one text only.

weeks.prep: Print Wheatley's 'On Being Brought from Africa to America' and her 1774 letter to Samson Occom; Abigail Adams' March 31, 1776 letter ('Remember the Ladies'); an excerpt of Washington's Farewell Address for the test.
misconceptions: Reading Wheatley's poem as simple gratitude for slavery. Show the turn in the last lines that commands 'Christians' to remember that Black people 'may be refin'd, and join th' angelic train' — she uses their religion to claim equality.
Summarizing instead of analyzing in a rhetorical analysis essay. Every body paragraph must name a choice, give an example, and explain its effect on the audience.

days.guide: Read the poem twice and the letter. Model analyzing how she addresses Christian readers on their own terms. Today's task from the plan: Read Wheatley's poem and Occom letter; analyze how she uses her audience's own beliefs to argue for freedom. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: How does Wheatley's poem use her audience's beliefs?
questions.a: She appeals to Christian teaching that all souls can be saved, warning readers that 'Negros, black as Cain, / May be refin'd, and join th' angelic train,' so they must accept Black people as spiritual equals.

questions.q: What contradiction does the Occom letter point out?
questions.a: That colonists cry for liberty while holding others in slavery; she says it does not take a philosopher to see these attitudes don't agree.

days.guide: Read the letter aloud. The student marks tone shifts (affectionate, playful, serious) and paraphrases the argument underneath. Today's task from the plan: Read 'Remember the Ladies'; identify tone shifts and the argument beneath the playful diction. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: What is Abigail Adams' argument beneath the playful threat to 'foment a Rebelion'?
questions.a: Women should have legal protections and a voice; she applies the Revolution's own principle (no laws without representation) to women and warns that 'all Men would be tyrants if they could.'

days.guide: The student chooses one founding-era text and outlines: situation, three rhetorical choices, effect of each. Today's task from the plan: Choose one founding-era text and outline a rhetorical analysis essay (situation, choices, effect). Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: What three parts should each body paragraph plan contain?
questions.a: The rhetorical choice (e.g., allusion), a quoted example, and an explanation of its effect on the specific audience and purpose.

days.guide: The student drafts 750 words. Teach punctuation: a colon introduces a quotation after a complete sentence; a semicolon joins two related independent clauses.

questions.q: Punctuate: Henry ends with a choice Give me liberty or give me death
questions.a: Henry ends with a stark choice: 'Give me liberty, or give me death!'

days.guide: Collect the revised essay; give the Unit 2 test with an unseen Farewell Address excerpt. Today's task from the plan: Revise and submit essay; Unit 2 test on rhetorical terms and an unseen passage (Washington's Farewell Address excerpt). Grade it the same day with the key below and have the student correct every missed item with a one-line note on what went wrong.

questions.q: What does Washington warn against in his Farewell Address?
questions.a: The dangers of political parties/factions and permanent alliances with foreign nations.

weeks.assessment_key: Rhetorical analysis rubric (4 = exceeds, 3 = proficient, 2 = developing, 1 = beginning) on four rows: Claim/Thesis (arguable, specific, answers the prompt); Evidence (well-chosen quotations, introduced and cited); Analysis/Reasoning (explains HOW evidence supports the claim, not just what it says); Conventions & organization (logical paragraphs, transitions, few errors). A proficient (3) paper identifies the speaker's situation and audience, analyzes at least three choices (e.g., Wheatley's biblical allusion to Cain, Adams' ironic threat of rebellion) with quotations, and explains how each serves the purpose. Unit 2 test key: ethos/pathos/logos definitions; parallelism; rhetorical question; allusion; syllogism. Unseen Farewell excerpt: purpose = to advise national unity; warns against faction and foreign entanglement; tone = paternal, earnest.

weeks.prep: Irving's 'The Devil and Tom Walker'; Poe's 'The Tell-Tale Heart' and 'The Fall of the House of Usher' (Gutenberg). Notes page on Romantic traits: emotion over reason, imagination, nature, the supernatural, the individual.
misconceptions: Confusing the narrator with the author. Poe was not a murderer; the unreliable narrator is a constructed character.
Thinking 'Romantic' means love stories. Literary Romanticism means valuing emotion, imagination, nature, and the individual.

days.guide: Give notes on Romanticism, then read Irving's story. The student marks satire of greed (Tom's usury, the 'devil take me' oath). Today's task from the plan: Take notes on Romantic traits; read 'The Devil and Tom Walker' and mark satire of greed. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: How does Tom Walker's end satirize greed?
questions.a: After swearing 'The devil take me if I have made a farthing!' he is carried off by the devil on a black horse, and his wealth turns to cinders and shavings — greed literally damns him and leaves nothing.

days.guide: Read 'The Tell-Tale Heart' aloud with expression. The student annotates evidence of unreliability and notes how short, exclamatory sentences build tension.

questions.q: How does the narrator's opening undercut his claim of sanity?
questions.a: He insists 'why will you say that I am mad?' while describing a 'very, very dreadfully nervous' state and a murder motivated by an old man's 'vulture eye'; his frantic protests prove the opposite.

questions.q: Why does the narrator confess?
questions.a: He hears what he thinks is the dead man's heart beating louder under the floor and, believing the police are mocking him, shrieks, 'I admit the deed!'

days.guide: Read 'Usher' (it is long; split with breaks). The student traces how the house (fissure, decay, reflection in the tarn) mirrors Roderick's mind. Today's task from the plan: Read 'The Fall of the House of Usher'; trace setting as a symbol of Roderick's mind. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: How does the house symbolize Roderick?
questions.a: Its decay and nearly invisible crack match his mental deterioration; when Madeline dies and Roderick collapses, the house splits along the fissure and sinks into the tarn.

days.guide: Explain Poe's 'unity of effect' (every detail builds toward one emotional impression). The student writes a paragraph on how one ending achieves it. Today's task from the plan: Write an analytical paragraph on how Poe's choice of ending structure produces 'unity of effect'. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: What is 'unity of effect'?
questions.a: Poe's idea that a short story should be read in one sitting and every element should build a single intended effect, such as terror.

days.guide: Give a 10-item quiz on Romantic/Gothic conventions, then a comparison paragraph of Irving's and Poe's narrators. Today's task from the plan: Quiz on Romantic/Gothic conventions; one-paragraph comparison of Irving's and Poe's narrators. Grade it the same day with the key below and have the student correct every missed item with a one-line note on what went wrong.

questions.q: Compare the narrators of 'Devil and Tom Walker' and 'Tell-Tale Heart.'
questions.a: Irving uses a humorous third-person storyteller who passes on local legend; Poe uses an unreliable first-person narrator whose voice creates horror.

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz key: Gothic conventions = gloomy settings, decay, madness, the supernatural, suspense, death; Romantic = emotion, imagination, nature, individual; unreliable narrator = one whose account cannot be trusted; satire = humor exposing folly; unity of effect = single emotional impression. Analytical paragraph rubric (4-point): claim about how the ending creates the effect; two quotations; analysis of structure (e.g., the rapid, repeated 'louder! louder!' leading to confession); conventions.

weeks.prep: Emerson's 'Self-Reliance' and 'Nature' (ch. 1) and Thoreau's Walden ch. 2 and 'Civil Disobedience' excerpts (Gutenberg). Plan a safe place for a solo 20-minute nature walk.
misconceptions: Thinking Transcendentalism means rejecting all society. Emerson and Thoreau valued intuition and nature but also engaged in public debate (lectures, abolition).
Assuming civil disobedience means any lawbreaking. Thoreau's idea is open, nonviolent refusal to obey an unjust law and accepting the penalty.

days.guide: Read 'Self-Reliance' excerpts. The student chooses five aphorisms and explains each in plain language. Today's task from the plan: Read excerpts of 'Self-Reliance'; select five aphorisms and explain each in plain language. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: Explain 'A foolish consistency is the hobgoblin of little minds.'
questions.a: Refusing to change your views just to look consistent is a small-minded fear; a thinking person should follow what they now believe even if it contradicts what they said before.

questions.q: Explain 'Whoso would be a man must be a nonconformist.'
questions.a: To be a full person you must think for yourself instead of following society's expectations.

days.guide: Read the 'transparent eye-ball' passage. After the walk, the student writes a journal entry imitating Emerson's style. Today's task from the plan: Read the 'transparent eyeball' passage from 'Nature'; take a 20-minute solo nature walk and write a journal entry in imitation. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: What does Emerson mean by 'I become a transparent eye-ball; I am nothing; I see all'?
questions.a: In nature his ego disappears; he becomes pure perception and feels united with the divine ('part or particle of God').

days.guide: Read 'Where I Lived.' The student lists Thoreau's arguments and tests 'Simplify, simplify' against a log of their own day. Today's task from the plan: Read 'Where I Lived, and What I Lived For'; list Thoreau's arguments for simplicity and test one against your own daily schedule. Grade it the same day with the key below and have the student correct every missed item with a one-line note on what went wrong.

questions.q: Why did Thoreau go to the woods?
questions.a: 'Because I wished to live deliberately, to front only the essential facts of life,' and see if he could learn what life had to teach.

days.guide: Read 'Civil Disobedience' excerpts. Trace 'That government is best which governs least' to 'governs not at all.' Connect to Gandhi and King. Today's task from the plan: Read excerpts; trace how Thoreau refines the term 'government' and connect to later activists. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: Why did Thoreau spend a night in jail?
questions.a: He refused to pay his poll tax to protest slavery and the Mexican-American War.

days.guide: Run a 20-minute Socratic seminar on smartphones with the parent; the student uses three quotations, then writes a 300-word argument. Today's task from the plan: Socratic seminar: 'Would Thoreau approve of smartphones?'; write a 300-word argument response. Grade it the same day with the key below and have the student correct every missed item with a one-line note on what went wrong.

questions.q: Give one quotation Thoreau might use against smartphones.
questions.a: 'Our life is frittered away by detail... Simplify, simplify' — constant notifications fill life with trivial detail.

weeks.assessment_key: Seminar rubric (4-point): cites Emerson/Thoreau at least three times, asks a question, responds to others' ideas, stays respectful. Short argument rubric: clear claim; at least two quotations from Walden or 'Self-Reliance' used accurately; a counterpoint (e.g., Thoreau valued learning and communication, so phones could serve deliberate living); conventions.

weeks.prep: Hawthorne's 'Young Goodman Brown' and 'The Minister's Black Veil' and Melville's 'Bartleby, the Scrivener' (Gutenberg).
misconceptions: Demanding a single answer to whether Brown dreamed the meeting. Hawthorne leaves it ambiguous ('Be it so if you will'); the point is the effect on Brown.
Seeing Bartleby as simply lazy. Focus on the narrator's reactions and the deadening Wall Street setting; the story asks what we owe each other.

days.guide: Read 'Young Goodman Brown.' The student annotates Faith's pink ribbons, the serpent-like staff, and the forest, then decides about the dream. Today's task from the plan: Read and annotate symbols (Faith's ribbons, staff, forest); decide whether the journey was a dream. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: What do Faith's pink ribbons symbolize, and why does it matter when one blows down?
questions.a: They suggest innocence/faith; when a ribbon falls from the sky, Brown believes his wife has joined the devil and cries, 'My Faith is gone!'

questions.q: How does the experience change Brown?
questions.a: He becomes stern, distrustful, and gloomy for life; 'his dying hour was gloom' because he sees sin in everyone.

days.guide: Read 'The Minister's Black Veil.' The student charts reactions (congregation, Elizabeth, the dying) and writes a paragraph on the veil's meaning. Today's task from the plan: Read 'The Minister's Black Veil'; chart the community's reactions and explain the veil's meaning in a paragraph. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: What does Hooper reveal on his deathbed?
questions.a: He says he sees 'on every visage a Black Veil' — everyone hides secret sin, and the veil only makes visible what all people conceal.

days.guide: Read the first half of 'Bartleby.' Discuss the narrator's 'safe' personality and what 'I would prefer not to' does. Today's task from the plan: Read the first half of 'Bartleby'; analyze the narrator's attitude and the phrase 'I would prefer not to'. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: Why is 'I would prefer not to' so disruptive?
questions.a: It is a polite refusal, not a defiance the narrator can argue with; it leaves him confused and powerless.

days.guide: Finish the story. The student makes a T-chart comparing Bartleby's refusal with Thoreau's. Today's task from the plan: Finish the story; compare Bartleby's refusal to Thoreau's civil disobedience in a T-chart. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: How does Bartleby's refusal differ from Thoreau's?
questions.a: Thoreau's refusal is purposeful protest with a stated cause; Bartleby gives no reason and withdraws entirely, ending in death in the Tombs.

days.guide: Timed essay (40 min): two Dark Romantic texts vs. Emerson's optimism. Today's task from the plan: Timed essay (40 min): How do two Dark Romantic texts challenge Emerson's optimism?. Grade it the same day with the key below and have the student correct every missed item with a one-line note on what went wrong.

questions.q: What is the core difference between Dark Romantics and Transcendentalists?
questions.a: Transcendentalists believe in human goodness and divine nature; Dark Romantics emphasize sin, guilt, and the darker side of human nature.

weeks.assessment_key: Timed comparative essay rubric (4 = exceeds, 3 = proficient, 2 = developing, 1 = beginning) on four rows: Claim/Thesis (arguable, specific, answers the prompt); Evidence (well-chosen quotations, introduced and cited); Analysis/Reasoning (explains HOW evidence supports the claim, not just what it says); Conventions & organization (logical paragraphs, transitions, few errors). A proficient (3) paper states how two texts challenge Emerson's belief in human goodness and self-trust (e.g., Brown's discovery of universal sin; Hooper's veil; Bartleby's isolation), quotes Emerson and both stories, and explains contrast, not just summary.

weeks.prep: Whitman's 'Song of Myself' sections 1, 6, 52 and 'I Hear America Singing'; Dickinson's 'Because I could not stop for Death,' 'Hope is the thing with feathers,' 'Tell all the truth but tell it slant,' and one more (Poetry Foundation).
misconceptions: Assuming Dickinson's dashes are mistakes. They are deliberate pauses that create hesitation and multiple readings.
Calling free verse 'random.' Whitman uses rhythm through anaphora, catalogs, and parallelism instead of meter.

days.guide: Read Whitman aloud. The student marks catalogs and anaphora and explains their effect. Today's task from the plan: Read 'Song of Myself' sections aloud; identify catalogs and anaphora and their effect. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: What does the catalog in 'I Hear America Singing' suggest?
questions.a: By listing mechanics, carpenters, masons, boatmen, shoemakers, and mothers, each singing 'what belongs to him or her,' Whitman celebrates democracy as many individuals together.

questions.q: How does Whitman answer death at the end of section 52?
questions.a: He bequeaths himself 'to the dirt to grow from the grass I love' and says 'look for me under your boot-soles' — death is a continuation into nature.

days.guide: Read four Dickinson poems. Model scanning common meter (alternating 8 and 6 syllables). The student paraphrases each. Today's task from the plan: Read four Dickinson poems; scan meter, mark dashes and slant rhymes, and paraphrase each. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: In 'Because I could not stop for Death,' how is Death portrayed?
questions.a: As a polite gentleman caller who 'kindly stopped' and drives the speaker in a carriage, with Immortality, toward eternity.

questions.q: Paraphrase 'Tell all the truth but tell it slant.'
questions.a: Truth is too bright to take all at once, so tell it indirectly ('Success in Circuit lies'); 'The Truth must dazzle gradually / Or every man be blind.'

days.guide: The student chooses death or the self and collects six quotations (three per poet). Today's task from the plan: Plan a comparison of how Whitman and Dickinson treat death or the self; collect six quotations. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: Give a contrast between Whitman and Dickinson on the self.
questions.a: Whitman's self is expansive and public ('I celebrate myself'); Dickinson's is private and compressed, exploring inner experience in short stanzas.

days.guide: The student drafts 600 words and practices recitation (12+ lines) for voice and pacing. Today's task from the plan: Draft a 600-word poetry comparison essay, then memorize and recite one poem (12+ lines). Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: What makes a strong recitation?
questions.a: Accurate memorization, clear pacing that follows punctuation (not line ends), and tone that matches meaning.

days.guide: Collect the essay and give the Unit 3 test. Today's task from the plan: Submit revised essay and take the Unit 3 test on Romantic and Transcendentalist texts. Grade it the same day with the key below and have the student correct every missed item with a one-line note on what went wrong.

questions.q: Define slant rhyme with an example.
questions.a: Near rhyme with similar but not identical sounds, e.g., 'soul / all' in 'Hope is the thing with feathers.'

weeks.assessment_key: Poetry comparison essay rubric (4 = exceeds, 3 = proficient, 2 = developing, 1 = beginning) on four rows: Claim/Thesis (arguable, specific, answers the prompt); Evidence (well-chosen quotations, introduced and cited); Analysis/Reasoning (explains HOW evidence supports the claim, not just what it says); Conventions & organization (logical paragraphs, transitions, few errors). A proficient (3) paper makes a comparative thesis about death or the self, uses three quotations from each poet, and analyzes form (Whitman's catalogs and free verse vs. Dickinson's dashes and common meter) as well as content. Recitation: 4 = accurate and expressive; 3 = minor slips; 2 = several prompts; 1 = read from page. Unit 3 test key: Romanticism, Transcendentalism, Dark Romanticism, unreliable narrator, symbol, free verse, slant rhyme, anaphora, catalog.

weeks.prep: Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass (Gutenberg). Parent note: depicts the brutal whipping of Douglass' Aunt Hester (Ch. 1) and other violence; read ahead and discuss.
misconceptions: Reading the Narrative as only a personal story. Douglass makes an argument against slavery; each episode is evidence.
Overlooking that slavery corrupts enslavers too. Track Sophia Auld's transformation.

days.guide: Read Garrison's preface and Ch. 1. Explain why prefaces by white abolitionists were used. Today's task from the plan: Read Garrison's preface and Douglass' Ch. 1; note how prefaces were used to authenticate narratives. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: Why did the Narrative open with Garrison's preface?
questions.a: White abolitionists' endorsements helped convince white readers that a formerly enslaved man really wrote it and that it was true.

questions.q: What does Douglass not know about himself, and why does it matter?
questions.a: His birthday and his father's identity; enslavers kept enslaved people ignorant to deny them identity.

days.guide: Read Ch. 2–4. The student records effects of slavery on the enslaved and the enslavers. Today's task from the plan: Read and record examples of slavery's effect on enslavers as well as the enslaved. Before the student writes conclusions, check that the data table has units and repeated trials, and ask them to explain one result in their own words.

questions.q: How do the slave songs reveal suffering?
questions.a: Douglass says the songs expressed deep sorrow, not happiness, which rebuts the claim that singing showed contentment.

days.guide: Read Ch. 5–6. Discuss Hugh Auld's prohibition and Douglass' realization. Today's task from the plan: Read about Baltimore and learning letters; explain why Douglass calls literacy 'the pathway from slavery to freedom'. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: Why does Douglass call literacy 'the pathway from slavery to freedom'?
questions.a: When Mr. Auld forbids reading because it would 'unfit him to be a slave,' Douglass realizes literacy gives power and freedom of mind.

questions.q: How does Sophia Auld change?
questions.a: Kind at first, she becomes cruel under slavery's power: her 'cheerful eye... soon became red with rage.'

days.guide: Model analysis of a balanced sentence or antithesis. The student writes a 300-word close reading. Today's task from the plan: Analyze one paragraph's diction and syntax (balanced sentences, antithesis) in a 300-word response. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: What is antithesis, and why does Douglass use it?
questions.a: Contrasting ideas in parallel structure; it makes contradictions of slavery and 'Christian' enslavers stark.

days.guide: Give a reading quiz on Ch. 1–6 and check the central-idea tracker. Today's task from the plan: Reading quiz Ch. 1–6 and central-idea tracker check. Grade it the same day with the key below and have the student correct every missed item with a one-line note on what went wrong.

questions.q: Why was Douglass sent to Baltimore and why does he call it fortunate?
questions.a: To live with Hugh and Sophia Auld; it opened the way to learning to read and to the city's relative freedom.

weeks.assessment_key: Reading quiz key: 1) Douglass born in Maryland. 2) Separated from his mother as an infant. 3) Aunt Hester's whipping = 'the blood-stained gate.' 4) Songs reveal sorrow. 5) Moved to Baltimore with the Aulds. 6) Sophia begins teaching him letters. 7) Hugh forbids it. 8) Douglass learns reading is the pathway to freedom. Close-reading rubric (4-point): identifies specific diction/syntax; quotes precisely; explains effect on argument; well organized.

weeks.prep: Narrative Ch. 7–11 and Appendix; Harriet Jacobs, Incidents ch. 21 'The Loophole of Retreat' (Gutenberg). Parent note: Jacobs discusses sexual harassment by her enslaver.
misconceptions: Thinking learning to read immediately made Douglass happy. He writes learning had been 'a curse rather than a blessing' because it made him aware of his condition.
Assuming the narratives make identical appeals. Jacobs targets Northern white women's sense of domestic virtue and motherhood.

days.guide: Read Ch. 7–9. The student tracks how Douglass learns from boys in the street and The Columbian Orator. Today's task from the plan: Read; identify how learning to read changes Douglass' self-understanding. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: How did Douglass learn to read and write after his lessons stopped?
questions.a: He traded bread for lessons from poor white boys, studied The Columbian Orator, and copied letters in the shipyard and from young Master Thomas's old copy-books.

questions.q: Why did reading also cause anguish?
questions.a: It let him understand his enslavement but offered no escape; he envied animals for not thinking.

days.guide: Read Ch. 10. Analyze the chiasmus and why it marks the book's turning point. Today's task from the plan: Read the Covey chapter; analyze the chiasmus 'You have seen how a man was made a slave...' and its placement. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: Explain 'You have seen how a man was made a slave; you shall see how a slave was made a man.'
questions.a: The reversed structure mirrors the reversal in his life: after fighting Covey, he regains his sense of manhood and resolves never to be a slave in spirit.

questions.q: What changed after the fight with Covey?
questions.a: Covey never whipped him again; Douglass says that though he remained a slave 'in form,' he would never be one 'in fact.'

days.guide: Finish the Narrative. Discuss why he hides escape details and what the Appendix argues. Today's task from the plan: Finish the Narrative; explain why Douglass withholds escape details and how the appendix addresses religion. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: Why does Douglass withhold how he escaped?
questions.a: Revealing methods would endanger those who helped him and alert enslavers, closing routes for others.

questions.q: What does the Appendix clarify about religion?
questions.a: He opposes 'the slaveholding religion of this land,' not 'the pure, peaceable, and impartial Christianity of Christ.'

days.guide: Read the Jacobs excerpt. The student compares her appeals with Douglass'. Today's task from the plan: Read the 'loophole of retreat' excerpt; compare Jacobs' appeals to women readers with Douglass' appeals. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: What was the 'loophole of retreat'?
questions.a: A tiny crawl space in her grandmother's attic where Jacobs hid for about seven years, watching her children through a small hole.

days.guide: Record a 15-minute discussion; collect an exit response on structure. Today's task from the plan: Recorded discussion comparing the two narratives; written exit response on structure. Grade it the same day with the key below and have the student correct every missed item with a one-line note on what went wrong.

questions.q: How do the narratives' endings differ?
questions.a: Douglass ends with freedom and his work as an abolitionist speaker; Jacobs notes her story 'ends with freedom; not in the usual way, with marriage,' challenging domestic-novel expectations.

weeks.assessment_key: Discussion rubric (4-point): cites both narratives, compares appeals and structure, responds to questions. Exit response: proficient answer notes Douglass's chiastic turning point (Covey) and Jacobs's direct address to women readers.

weeks.prep: Douglass' 'What to the Slave Is the Fourth of July?'; Sojourner Truth's 1851 speech (Robinson version) and 1863 Gage version; Lincoln's Gettysburg Address and Second Inaugural. Phone for video.
misconceptions: Quoting 'Ain't I a Woman?' as Truth's exact words. The most-quoted version was published by Frances Gage 12 years later with added Southern dialect; the 1851 report lacks that refrain.
Reading the Second Inaugural as a victory speech. Lincoln emphasizes shared guilt, humility, and reconciliation.

days.guide: Read the central section of Douglass's speech. The student charts how he moves from praising the founders to indicting the nation. Today's task from the plan: Read the central section; chart how Douglass turns the audience's celebration into an indictment. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: What answer does Douglass give to 'What, to the American slave, is your 4th of July?'
questions.a: 'A day that reveals to him... the gross injustice and cruelty to which he is the constant victim'; the celebration is a 'sham.'

questions.q: Why does Douglass say 'This Fourth of July is yours, not mine'?
questions.a: Freedom celebrated by white Americans excludes enslaved people; he forces the audience to see the hypocrisy.

days.guide: Read both Truth versions side by side. The student lists differences and discusses how editing shapes voice. Today's task from the plan: Compare the 1851 Robinson transcription with the 1863 Gage version; discuss how editing changed her voice. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: Name two ways Gage's 1863 version differs from the 1851 report.
questions.a: Gage added the repeated refrain 'Ain't I a woman?' and a heavy Southern dialect, though Truth was from New York and spoke Dutch first.

days.guide: Read both Lincoln texts. The student marks antithesis and biblical allusion and explains the shift in purpose. Today's task from the plan: Read the Gettysburg Address and Second Inaugural; mark antithesis and biblical allusion and explain the shift in purpose. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: Find an antithesis in the Second Inaugural.
questions.a: 'Both read the same Bible and pray to the same God; and each invokes His aid against the other.'

questions.q: How do the purposes differ?
questions.a: Gettysburg honors the dead and asks the living to finish the work so government 'of the people, by the people, for the people' survives; the Second Inaugural frames the war as judgment for slavery and calls for reconciliation 'with malice toward none.'

days.guide: The student memorizes and delivers the Gettysburg Address or a 2-minute excerpt with deliberate pauses; review the video. Today's task from the plan: Memorize and deliver the Gettysburg Address or a 2-minute excerpt with deliberate pauses; self-evaluate from video. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: Where should the speaker pause in 'we can not dedicate—we can not consecrate—we can not hallow—this ground'?
questions.a: At each dash, so the three parallel verbs build to 'this ground.'

days.guide: Timed 40-minute rhetorical analysis of the Second Inaugural. Today's task from the plan: Timed rhetorical analysis (40 min) of the Second Inaugural. Grade it the same day with the key below and have the student correct every missed item with a one-line note on what went wrong.

questions.q: What is the purpose of 'With malice toward none, with charity for all'?
questions.a: To call the nation to reconcile and 'bind up the nation's wounds' rather than punish the South.

weeks.assessment_key: Delivery rubric (4-point): memorization, pacing and pauses, volume/clarity, eye contact. Timed analysis rubric: proficient essay explains Lincoln's purpose (reconciliation and moral reckoning) and analyzes antithesis, biblical allusion ('judge not, that we be not judged'), and the long sentence on 'every drop of blood drawn with the lash' with effect on a war-weary audience.

weeks.prep: Unit 4 texts. Optional: excerpt from the 1858 Lincoln-Douglas debates (Ottawa or Freeport) for the test.
misconceptions: Confusing evidence with warrant. Evidence is the quotation; the warrant explains why it proves the claim.
Writing comma splices ('Douglass praised the founders, he condemned slavery'). Fix with a period, semicolon, or conjunction.

days.guide: Discuss the prompt. The student writes a claim and gathers evidence from three Unit 4 texts. Today's task from the plan: Respond to 'Did the founding documents contain the seeds of abolition?' Draft a claim and gather evidence from three Unit 4 texts. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: Give one piece of evidence that the founding documents contained the 'seeds of abolition.'
questions.a: Douglass in the Fourth of July speech calls the Constitution 'a GLORIOUS LIBERTY DOCUMENT' and appeals to the Declaration's principles.

days.guide: Model one claim-reason-evidence-warrant chain. The student builds a full outline with counterclaim and rebuttal. Today's task from the plan: Build an outline with claim, reasons, evidence, warrants, and a counterclaim with rebuttal. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: What is a strong counterclaim?
questions.a: The Constitution protected slavery (the three-fifths clause and the fugitive slave clause), so the founders did not intend abolition.

days.guide: Teach parallel structure in thesis and topic sentences. The student drafts 900 words. Today's task from the plan: Write a 900-word argument essay; grammar focus: parallel structure in thesis and topic sentences. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: Fix the parallelism: 'Douglass used irony, questions that were rhetorical, and he appealed to the founders.'
questions.a: 'Douglass used irony, rhetorical questions, and appeals to the founders.'

days.guide: Parent reviews with the rubric. The student revises warrants and transitions and fixes comma splices. Today's task from the plan: Peer/parent review with a rubric; revise for warrants and transitions; edit for comma splices. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: Fix: 'Lincoln spoke briefly, the speech became famous.'
questions.a: 'Lincoln spoke briefly, yet the speech became famous.' or 'Lincoln spoke briefly; the speech became famous.'

days.guide: Collect the final essay; give the Unit 4 test with an unseen Lincoln-Douglas debate passage. Today's task from the plan: Submit the final essay and take the Unit 4 test (unseen passage from Lincoln-Douglas debates). Grade it the same day with the key below and have the student correct every missed item with a one-line note on what went wrong.

questions.q: What was Stephen Douglas's 'popular sovereignty'?
questions.a: Letting settlers of each territory vote on whether to allow slavery.

weeks.assessment_key: Argument essay rubric (4 = exceeds, 3 = proficient, 2 = developing, 1 = beginning) on four rows: Claim/Thesis (arguable, specific, answers the prompt); Evidence (well-chosen quotations, introduced and cited); Analysis/Reasoning (explains HOW evidence supports the claim, not just what it says); Conventions & organization (logical paragraphs, transitions, few errors). A proficient (3) paper takes a clear position, uses evidence from three texts (Douglass, Lincoln, the Declaration/Constitution), explains warrants, and rebuts a real counterclaim (e.g., the three-fifths and fugitive slave clauses). Unit 4 test key: Lincoln argues slavery is a moral wrong whose spread must be stopped; Douglas argues popular sovereignty; identify antithesis, appeals, and Douglass's Fourth of July irony.

weeks.prep: Twain's 'The Notorious Jumping Frog of Calaveras County' and Huckleberry Finn ch. 1, 16, 31 (Gutenberg); two short critical views on teaching Huck Finn. Parent note: the novel uses the n-word frequently; discuss before reading.
misconceptions: Thinking Twain endorses Huck's society's racism. Twain uses Huck's naive voice to satirize it; the irony depends on readers seeing what Huck can't.
Mixing up Realism and Romanticism. Realism portrays ordinary life, regional speech, and believable characters.

days.guide: Give notes on Realism. Read 'The Jumping Frog.' The student identifies the frame narrative. Today's task from the plan: Notes on Realism vs. Romanticism; read 'The Jumping Frog' (a California story) and identify the frame narrative. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: What is the frame of 'The Jumping Frog'?
questions.a: An educated narrator asks Simon Wheeler about Leonidas W. Smiley; Wheeler instead tells a long tale about Jim Smiley and his frog Dan'l Webster.

questions.q: How did the stranger win the bet?
questions.a: He filled Dan'l Webster with quail shot so the frog was too heavy to jump.

days.guide: Read ch. 1 and 16. The student marks examples of Huck's vernacular creating humor and irony. Today's task from the plan: Read; analyze how Huck's vernacular voice creates humor and irony. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: What happens in ch. 16 when men looking for runaways approach the raft?
questions.a: Huck plans to turn Jim in, but instead lets the men believe his family has smallpox, so they leave money and flee — he protects Jim.

days.guide: Read ch. 31. Explain the irony of 'All right, then, I'll go to hell.' Today's task from the plan: Read the climax of Huck's conscience; explain the irony of his decision. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: Why is Huck's decision ironic?
questions.a: He believes helping Jim is a sin, but the reader sees it is the moral choice; his conscience, shaped by a slaveholding society, is wrong.

days.guide: Read two critical views. The student writes a 300-word position on teaching the novel. Today's task from the plan: Read two short critical views on teaching the novel; write a 300-word position response. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: What is one argument for and one against teaching the novel?
questions.a: For: its satire exposes racism. Against: the repeated slur and Jim's stereotyped portrayal can harm readers.

days.guide: Quiz on Realism and satire; paragraph on the irony of ch. 31. Today's task from the plan: Quiz on Realism terms and satire; paragraph on the irony in Ch. 31. Grade it the same day with the key below and have the student correct every missed item with a one-line note on what went wrong.

questions.q: Define satire.
questions.a: Humor, irony, or exaggeration used to expose and criticize foolishness or vice.

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz key: Realism = truthful depiction of ordinary life; local color/regionalism = dialect and customs of a region; vernacular = everyday speech; frame narrative = story within a story; satire. Irony paragraph rubric: thesis on the gap between Huck's belief and moral reality; quotation of 'All right, then, I'll go to hell'; explanation of Twain's target.

weeks.prep: Chopin 'The Story of an Hour,' Bierce 'Occurrence at Owl Creek Bridge,' Gilman 'The Yellow Wallpaper,' London 'To Build a Fire' (Gutenberg/CommonLit). Parent note: hanging, mental illness, and death.
misconceptions: Reading the doctors in Chopin as correct that Louise died of 'joy that kills.' The irony is that she died of shock at losing her freedom.
Thinking Naturalism and Realism are identical. Naturalism adds that heredity, environment, and nature's indifference determine fate.

days.guide: Read 'The Story of an Hour.' The student annotates the window imagery and explains the ending. Today's task from the plan: Read 'The Story of an Hour'; annotate the open window imagery and explain the final irony. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: What does the open window represent?
questions.a: New life and freedom: she sees 'the tops of trees that were all aquiver with the new spring life.'

questions.q: Explain the final irony.
questions.a: Doctors say she died 'of joy that kills,' but readers know she died from the shock of losing newfound freedom when Brently walks in.

days.guide: Read 'Owl Creek Bridge.' The student diagrams Parts I–III. Today's task from the plan: Read 'Owl Creek Bridge'; diagram the three-part structure and analyze the manipulation of time. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: Describe the three-part structure.
questions.a: I: Farquhar about to be hanged on the bridge. II: flashback showing a Federal scout tricked him. III: an apparent escape that is a fantasy in the moment before death.

days.guide: Read 'The Yellow Wallpaper.' The student tracks the narrator's wallpaper descriptions. Today's task from the plan: Read 'The Yellow Wallpaper'; track the narrator's changing descriptions of the wallpaper. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: What is the narrator's 'rest cure,' and how does it affect her?
questions.a: Her physician husband John forbids work; isolation pushes her into psychosis, believing a woman is trapped behind the wallpaper.

days.guide: Read 'To Build a Fire.' The student lists Naturalist ideas and contrasts with Emerson. Today's task from the plan: Read 'To Build a Fire'; identify Naturalist ideas about nature and fate; compare to Emerson's 'Nature'. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: What is the man's fatal flaw?
questions.a: He lacks imagination and ignores the old-timer's warning; nature is indifferent.

days.guide: The student writes a 600-word explanatory essay on structure. Today's task from the plan: Write a 600-word explanatory essay on how two of these authors use structure to create a surprise ending. Grade it the same day with the key below and have the student correct every missed item with a one-line note on what went wrong.

questions.q: Why does Bierce use a flashback in Part II?
questions.a: To explain how Farquhar got there and delay the ending, making the fantasy in Part III believable.

weeks.assessment_key: Explanatory essay on structure rubric (4 = exceeds, 3 = proficient, 2 = developing, 1 = beginning) on four rows: Claim/Thesis (arguable, specific, answers the prompt); Evidence (well-chosen quotations, introduced and cited); Analysis/Reasoning (explains HOW evidence supports the claim, not just what it says); Conventions & organization (logical paragraphs, transitions, few errors). A proficient (3) paper explains how two authors build toward a surprise ending (e.g., Chopin's compressed hour and final irony; Bierce's chronology shift and dream sequence), with two quotations from each.

weeks.prep: Assemble the semester reading journal and essays. Make a practice set of two unseen passages (e.g., a Dickinson poem not studied and a Thoreau paragraph) with questions. Plan two exam days.
misconceptions: Memorizing period names without traits or texts. Every period on the timeline needs traits AND an example quotation.
Writing a synthesis essay that summarizes each text in turn. Organize by idea, using several texts in each paragraph.

days.guide: The student builds a timeline: Puritan, Revolutionary/Enlightenment, Romantic, Transcendentalist, Dark Romantic, Realism/Naturalism, with two texts, traits, and one quotation each.

questions.q: Give the traits and one text for Transcendentalism.
questions.a: Intuition, self-reliance, nature as divine, nonconformity; Emerson's 'Self-Reliance' ('Trust thyself').

days.guide: Complete the practice passages timed; review answers. Today's task from the plan: Complete a practice set of unseen prose and poetry passages with multiple choice and short response. Use the questions below as a quick oral check; if an answer is shaky, reteach with one more example before moving on.

questions.q: What strategy helps on unseen poetry?
questions.a: Read twice, paraphrase each stanza, note shifts (words like 'but'), then answer using exact lines.

days.guide: The student revises the weakest essay and writes a reflection. Today's task from the plan: Revise the weakest essay of the semester using teacher comments; write a reflection on growth. questions.q: What should the growth reflection include?
questions.a: Specific skills improved (e.g., warrants), evidence from essays, and one goal for next semester.

days.guide: Exam I: three unseen passages with multiple choice and short responses, 60 minutes. questions.q: What makes a strong short constructed response?
questions.a: A direct answer, one or two short quotations, and a sentence explaining how the evidence supports the answer.

days.guide: Exam II: 50-minute synthesis essay on how American writers defined freedom. questions.q: Name three texts with different views of freedom.
questions.a: Henry: political liberty; Thoreau: freedom of conscience; Douglass: literacy and self-ownership; Chopin: personal freedom from marriage.

weeks.assessment_key: Exam I: score multiple choice by key; short responses on a 2-point scale. Exam II rubric (4-point): thesis about how definitions of freedom changed; at least four texts across periods; organized by idea; accurate quotations. Portfolio: revised essay shows substantive changes.

weeks.prep: Print 'Prufrock,' Pound's 'In a Station of the Metro,' Williams' 'The Red Wheelbarrow,' Frost's 'Mending Wall' and 'The Road Not Taken.' A one-page WWI/Modernism overview.

Expecting Modernist poems to state a clear message. Fragmentation and allusion are the point: they reflect a broken, uncertain world.

days.guide: Give notes on Modernism. Read Imagist poems. The student writes two Imagist poems. Today's task from the plan: Notes on WWI, urbanization, and Modernism; read Imagist poems by Pound and Williams and write two Imagist poems of your own.
